# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([merge-to-main/SKILL.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.

   run it whichever way step 4 went — a failed run is the one most worth having a record of:


   knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that contributes none does nothing.

   which is precisely the ending that fires no `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every
   unattended run would leave no record of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not
   of the checks that caught something, not of how the work actually went. Run it here and it

1	# Growth — dedup local packs against the canon (per repo)
2	
3	The growth lifecycle's pruning stage: reconcile this repo's **local packs** against the shared **canon** it
4	consumes (Claudinite, vendored read-only), pruning local items — a pack's prose line, or a whole local check —
5	the canon now covers. It opens a PR against the repo's default branch for the owner to approve. Often there's
6	nothing to prune, and that's fine. You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue, whose
7	**Context** is **binding scope — not a hint** (the executor will not let you re-decide or widen it).
8	
9	> This task only prunes local packs against the canon; lifting local items up into the canon is the central
10	> promote task's job (canon-side).
11	
12	## Conventions used in this doc
13	
14	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
15	- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Updating the tracking issue and opening the PR go through the session's
16	  **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub access — the shell reaches
17	  only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so never reach for `gh`/`curl` or
18	  a cross-repo clone.
19	- **The mounted canon.** The exact canon revision this repo currently consumes — compare against *that*, not a
20	  live fetch. It is what `.claudinite/shared/` holds at the mount's stamp (a promotion is visible here only
21	  once baselining has converged the mount to include it). Prune only against what the repo actually mounts.
22	- **The dispatch's Context narrows the *yardstick*, never the local surface.** When the Context names
23	  newly-changed canon packs ("Re-check local items against these newly-changed canon packs: …"), **those packs
24	  are this run's entire yardstick**: every prune must cite a line or rule id from one of *them*, and you never
25	  widen the comparison to the rest of the mounted canon. What is *not* narrowed is the local side — **every**
26	  local item is in play against those packs, whatever it is about. (Local pack names are unrelated to canon
27	  pack names, so there is nothing to match up.) A dispatch with **no** Context block carries no such bound: the
28	  precondition emits the list only when the mounted canon moved, and its other arm — the repo's own local packs
29	  changed — deliberately emits none, so that run compares the fresh local items against the whole mounted canon.
30	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) —
31	  everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the
32	  rename window). That's the corpus this task prunes within; the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under
33	  `.claudinite/` is never a prune target, only the yardstick you prune *against*.
34	
35	## What it does: prune / rephrase local packs the canon now covers
36	
37	When the canon has **absorbed** a practice a local doc still carries — most often an item the central promote
38	task lifted up and the canon now owns — the local copy is redundant. This task:
39	
40	- **Removes** the now-duplicated local item, since the canon is the single source of truth for portable rules.
41	- **Strips** a *partially* covered item down to its residue — when an item's general half is now canon-owned
42	  but it still carries a stronger point about a narrower case, **delete the portable half in place and keep
43	  only the residue**. A strip is a **deletion that shrinks the entry**: lead with the residual point (using the
44	  file's own `(canon)` tag convention if it has one), never with a meta-line like "this rule is portable
45	  (canon)", and **never re-state the now-canon rule, its fix, or which pack owns it** — carrying it is exactly
46	  what you are removing. If your "strip" adds words or restates the canon, you have *un*-deduped the item: keep
47	  the pre-edit text instead.
48	- **Rephrases** a local procedure *only* when the canon's wording of the same idea has changed, so the local
49	  packs stay consistent with the canon they point at — a rephrase tracks a wording drift; it never grows the
50	  entry and never re-imports canon prose.
51	
52	**Keep a local item only if it says *more* than the canon — not merely says it more specifically.** Every
53	local item is more specific than the canon, so specificity alone is never the test. Distinguish two cases:
54	
55	- **The general rule in local dress** — it makes the canon's point but leans on this repo's classes, files, or
56	  names to make it. Once the canon covers the point, those names were only illustration: prune it.
57	- **A stronger point about a narrower case** — it asserts something the canon's general rule leaves out: a
58	  tighter constraint, a sharper claim that holds for this repo's narrower situation. Keep it.
59	
60	So ask not "is it specific" (it always is) but "does it only lean on specific names to make the general point,
61	or does it make a point the canon doesn't?" Prune the first; keep the second.
62	
63	## A canon check covers an item too — and more strongly than prose
64	
65	The canon carries rules as **conformance checks**, not only prose. A local item is covered when a canon check
66	*enforces* it — stronger coverage than a stated line, since the rule runs on every session and CI pass.
67	Consult the machine-readable rule catalog (`node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs --list`:
68	id, severity, description, doc pointer — it lists the active local packs' own checks too) alongside the prose
69	corpus, and when a check covers the item, **quote the rule id** where you'd otherwise quote a canon line. This
70	cuts both ways: a **local pack's own check** is redundant once a canon check enforces the same rule — prune the
71	local `.mjs` (and drop it from `pack.mjs` + its fixture) exactly as you'd prune a duplicated prose line. The
72	keep-test above is unchanged: a local item that says *more* than the check detects (a stronger point about a
73	narrower case) stays.
74	
75	## Discipline
76	
77	- **Only remove a local item you can show the mounted canon genuinely covers — quote the canon line (or the
78	  covering check's rule id).** When unsure, leave it; a wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson.
79	- **Open a single PR against `main`** from a per-run-unique branch (see
80	  [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)) — one PR for the
81	  whole run's prunes, not one per item — never a direct push. This is an unattended task, on a capable model, and a **wrongful prune

59	
60	So ask not "is it specific" (it always is) but "does it only lean on specific names to make the general point,
61	or does it make a point the canon doesn't?" Prune the first; keep the second.
62	
63	## A canon check covers an item too — and more strongly than prose
64	
65	The canon carries rules as **conformance checks**, not only prose. A local item is covered when a canon check
66	*enforces* it — stronger coverage than a stated line, since the rule runs on every session and CI pass.
67	Consult the machine-readable rule catalog (`node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs --list`:
68	id, severity, description, doc pointer — it lists the active local packs' own checks too) alongside the prose
69	corpus, and when a check covers the item, **quote the rule id** where you'd otherwise quote a canon line. This
70	cuts both ways: a **local pack's own check** is redundant once a canon check enforces the same rule — prune the
71	local `.mjs` (and drop it from `pack.mjs` + its fixture) exactly as you'd prune a duplicated prose line. The
72	keep-test above is unchanged: a local item that says *more* than the check detects (a stronger point about a
73	narrower case) stays.
74	
75	## Discipline
76	
77	- **Only remove a local item you can show the mounted canon genuinely covers — quote the canon line (or the
78	  covering check's rule id).** When unsure, leave it; a wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson.
79	- **Open a single PR against `main`** from a per-run-unique branch (see
80	  [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)) — one PR for the
81	  whole run's prunes, not one per item — never a direct push. This is an unattended task, on a capable model, and a **wrongful prune
82	  deletes a real local lesson**, so — unlike [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md), whose additive edits
83	  ride a PR delivered to land after CI — this task keeps a **human** approval gate (its declared outcome ceiling
84	  is `open-pr`: it may open a PR but never merge it). **Put the issue reference in the commit message** —
85	  `Refs #<n>` for this task's tracking issue (below), in the commit itself, not only the PR body. The repo's
86	  `basics` `task-lifecycle` check gates a PR on its commits referencing an issue, so a prune commit that cites
87	  none reds the repo's CI and blocks the merge.
88	- If an edit touches something a test reads, run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green before pushing.
89	
90	## Tracking
91	
92	The task's standing log is the issue titled exactly, in this repo:
93	
94	> **Claudinite tracker: Growth Dedup**
95	
96	Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**. A run that finds no issue under
97	the exact title just creates one (closed). **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no
98	meaning, only the log does. Log each run that changed a doc as a **dated comment** — naming what was pruned and
99	the canon line that now covers it. A run that prunes nothing logs nothing.
100	
101	## Run on a capable model
102	
103	Proving the mounted canon genuinely covers a local item before pruning it — and telling "the canon now owns
104	this" from "the canon states this too generally, keep the local cut" — is a **judgment call**. A downgraded
105	model prunes a real lesson; the review PR is a backstop, but a wrongful prune is easy to wave through in
106	review, so don't lean on it. This task declares `agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
107	
108	## What this task must never do
109	
110	- **Never edit the read-only canon** — it only prunes the repo's *local packs* against it.
111	- **Never merge its own PR** — the human approval gate is the whole point (`outcome: open-pr`).
112	- **Never prune a local item without quoting the mounted-canon line (or covering check rule id) that covers
113	  it** — when unsure, leave it.
114	- **Never widen the dispatch's Context.** If it named the changed canon packs, a prune citing coverage from
115	  any *other* canon pack is out of scope for this run — leave the item; the cycle that moves that pack will
116	  reach it.
117	- **Never prune a local item that makes a stronger point about a narrower case** than the canon — that isn't
118	  redundancy. (A local item that only restates the canon in repo-specific names *is* prunable once the canon
119	  covers the point.)
120	- **Never let a dedup edit grow an entry or re-import canon prose.** Every action this task takes *removes*
121	  portable text: a Remove deletes the item, a Strip deletes its portable half, a Rephrase tracks a wording
122	  drift without adding. An edit that leaves an entry the same size or larger, re-quotes the now-canon rule, or
123	  names the owning pack's fix is a **corruption, not a dedup** — the exact inverse of the job. When in doubt
124	  about a kept item, leave it byte-for-byte unchanged rather than "reconcile" its wording. The
125	  `dedup-prune-integrity` check (`basics`-style work-scope rule, this pack) is the backstop: it reds the
126	  session when a dedup-labeled commit grows a local-pack prose file, or when any change adds a line that
127	  restates a canon rule ("… is portable (canon)", "… pack owns …").

1	# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)
2	
3	The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
4	committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
5	under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
6	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
7	[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
8	judgment those two don't carry.
9	
10	## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it
11	
12	`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy
13	(403 at the CONNECT). So: no session — this one included —
14	can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
15	runs through a sanctioned workflow: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
16	(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), `Fetch ticket prices (one-off)`
17	(`prices.yml`), or the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets` scheduled tasks.
18	Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
19	returns — either have a sanctioned workflow run it, or say plainly that it is
20	unverified.
21	
22	The egress block is a **policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around**. Do
23	not create ad-hoc GitHub Actions workflows — push-triggered "probes" or
24	anything else — to reach the API (or any blocked host) from an open-network
25	runner: that is CI as a side channel around the session's network rules.
26	
27	For one-off API questions (a field's shape, an enum's value set, whether an
28	operation exists at all), `scraper/SCRAPING.md` is the reference. When it falls
29	short there is one legitimate source short of asking the owner:
30	**`www.edfringe.com` itself is reachable**, and its Next.js bundles carry the
31	client's complete GraphQL operation set — every query, mutation and fragment,
32	with full field selections. Recipe in SCRAPING.md ("Reaching it from a Claude
33	Code web session"). That is reading a public asset from an allowed host, and it
34	is how the "no bulk price endpoint" claim was finally settled. It tells you what
35	a query would look like, never what it returns — so a change checked only that
36	way is still unverified against live data and must be reported as such. If that
37	doesn't answer it either, ask the repo owner rather than building a bypass.
38	
39	`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
40	offline; it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a
41	normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. Because
42	it is the only offline verification a scraper change can get, it must stay wired
43	into `scripts/verify.sh` — the `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` check
44	enforces that (a step *label* naming the self-test does not count; only a command
45	line does).
46	
47	## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean
48	
49	"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
50	`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
51	sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
52	`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
53	(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
54	availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
55	carried through for display only.
56	
57	## A price belongs to a performance, not to a show
58	
59	The same run sells at several prices: previews cheaper than the main run,
60	weekends dearer than weekdays. The first price pass didn't know that — it
61	called `performancePrices` for **one** performance per show and filed the answer
62	under the show. Pre-festival the performance it picked was almost always the
63	earliest, i.e. a preview, so **1,016 of 3,664 priced shows (28%) published their
64	cheapest night as their price**: Alfie Brown's £15/£16 run shipped as £8.50.
65	
66	The fix is not a rule about previews, and adding a "skip previews" or
67	"price after date X" heuristic re-creates the same class of bug from a different
68	angle — it still picks one performance and hopes it represents the rest.
69	**Price every performance.** There is no bulk price *field*, but GraphQL aliases
70	make one request carry a whole show's run (`fetch_prices.prices_query`), so full
71	per-night pricing costs roughly the same ~3,700 requests as the old pass. There
72	is no call budget to economise against here, so don't design as if there were.
73	
74	Which payload gets which number is the load-bearing distinction:
75	
76	| payload | question it answers | price |
77	|---|---|---|
78	| master, `shows.min.json` (planner) | what does this *show* cost? | run-wide `priceMin`..`priceMax` |
79	| `data/days/*.json` (Now page) | what does it cost *tonight*? | that performance's own `pm` |
80	
81	A performance the cache has no entry for gets **no `pm` at all** — "Price TBC" —
82	rather than the show's minimum. Borrowing a neighbouring night's figure is
83	exactly the bug above, and a lower bound presented as the price is a lie about
84	money even when every number in it is real.
85	
86	## Prices are fetched once, and "unknown" is a third state the encoding must keep
87	
88	`data/prices.json` is a fetch-once cache (`scraper/fetch_prices.py`), off the
89	nightly path: a show's price bands are set when it goes on sale, unlike its
90	ticket status. `refresh-shows` reads the cache and carries the amounts through
91	untouched — it never re-fetches them. So the festival keeps adding shows the
92	cache has never seen, and **a show with no price is a normal, permanent state of
93	the data**, not a gap the pipeline should close.
94	
95	The cache carries two entry shapes and both must stay readable: current entries
96	have `sets` + `perfs` (per performance), and entries from the old pass have a
97	bare whole-show `min`/`max`. The migration completes one show per re-run, so
98	dropping the legacy shape — or emptying the cache to "start clean" — would blank
99	every price on the site until a full pass finished. `price_sets` reads both.
100	
101	Which means the encoding carries three states, not two, and every stage has to
102	preserve the distinction:
103	
104	| state | master | wire |
105	|---|---|---|
106	| costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
107	| priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
108	| unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |
109	
110	`priceMin: 0` and `free: true` are **not** the same claim and don't always agree.
111	The flag comes from the listing; the £0 can also come from the price API, which
112	returns a single `Price band 1` at £0.00 for a handful of shows the listing
113	doesn't flag free — pay-what-you-want, or a box office that never set a price
114	(10 of 3,664 in the first full run). Both readings are honest about what a ticket
115	costs, so the price path keys off `priceMin`, and `free` stays what the *listing*
116	said. Don't "fix" one to match the other.
117	
118	Never encode unknown as `0`, and never let a decoder default it to one: a stage
119	that collapses three states into two is lying about money, and nothing
120	downstream can recover the difference. What the site then *does* with an unknown
121	price is a product decision, not a pipeline one — it lives in `shared/price.js`.
122	
123	Two traps in the raw price payload, both already handled and both worth not
124	re-introducing: amounts arrive as **strings**, and nearly every show carries a
125	£0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession (a carer's companion ticket) that must not
126	be read as the cheapest price. See the pricing section of
127	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md).
128	
129	## The API stamps performances in UTC — cross the zone once, at the edge
130	
131	The listing API's `dateTime` is a real UTC instant (`"2026-08-06T11:45:00.000Z"`),
132	**not** Edinburgh wall-clock with a decorative `Z`. Slicing the digits out of that
133	string is the trap: it looks like it works — every date and time in it is
134	plausible — and in August it is silently an hour wrong for the whole catalogue.
135	That is exactly what shipped, and what #275 cost to undo: 60,115 performances
136	listed an hour early, with the tell being shows that name their own time (a 10am
137	"Shakespeare for Breakfast" sitting at 09:00).
138	
139	The pipeline has **one** time-zone crossing, and it is `normalize.local_date_start`.
140	`refresh_ticket_status.py` and `fetch_prices.py` share it so a performance is keyed
141	by the same local date and start everywhere. Everything written after it — the
142	master, `data/days/*.json`, `availability.min.json`, `shows.min.json` — is already
143	Edinburgh wall-clock, so **no stage downstream parses, converts, or re-offsets a
144	time**. Treating a stored value as UTC a second time is the same bug from the other
145	end.
146	
147	Two consequences to hold on to when touching this:
148	
149	- **A "now" compared against these times is read in Edinburgh too** — `js/clock.js`
150	  (`festivalNow` / `festivalDate`), never the device clock. A UK visitor cannot see
151	  the difference, which is why a device clock survives review; a visitor planning
152	  from another zone reintroduces the whole drift.
153	- **A conversion change is a full-snapshot change.** The committed data is generator
154	  output, so the fix is not complete until the master is rebuilt through the new
155	  conversion and every derived artifact regenerated from it. Shifting the boundary
156	  moves performances between day files (two late 31 Aug performances now fall into
157	  1 Sep, outside the August day files, and live only in the master and the planner's
158	  catalogue) — expect that and check it, rather than reading it as data loss.
159	
160	## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it
161	
162	`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
163	`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
164	fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
165	`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
166	full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
167	`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.
168	
169	`data/prices.json` is the one exception, and it is an exception to the *direction*
170	rather than the rule: it is committed, but it is normalize.py's **input**, written
171	by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`. Nothing regenerates it on a schedule, so nothing
172	overwrites a hand-edit either — which is precisely why editing it by hand is still
173	wrong: the edit survives, silently disagreeing with the box office forever. Re-run
174	the fetch. The `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` check allows it **by name**,
175	so a second file can't ride in on its shape.
176	
177	## Changing the wire format is a four-file change
178	
179	The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
180	**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`). That
181	encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:
182	
183	- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
184	  `minify_master` / `build_availability`)
185	- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
186	- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
187	  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
188	  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`
189	
190	Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
191	indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
192	catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
193	decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.
194	
195	Two properties of that encoding are load-bearing for caching, and both fail
196	silently:
197	
198	- **The lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). The browser holds
199	  `shows.min.json` for four days and `venues.json` for one, so a stale catalogue
200	  is routinely decoded against a newer lookup file. An entry that changed index
201	  would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never
202	  dropped, even once the master stops using them.
203	- **`shows.min.json` carries nothing that changes through the day.** Ticket
204	  status lives in `availability.min.json` (its own status list, indexing into
205	  nothing, so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone). Putting a status back in
206	  the catalogue would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for
207	  anyone holding a cached copy — the bug in #249, re-created from the other end.
208	  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.
209	
210	The same three-way move applies to plain (non-indexed) wire keys such as the
211	price fields `pm` / `px`, with one extra hazard: the round-trip test compares the
212	rehydrated record to the master **as JSON**, so a new master key has to appear in
213	the *same position* in `normalize_event`'s dict and in `rehydrateShows`'s object
214	literal. Adding it in one place and appending it in the other fails the
215	round-trip on key order alone, which reads as a data bug and isn't one.

1	# EdFringeNow — project working rules
2	
3	Lessons captured while working in this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
4	canon. Terse and concrete; read the matching one before working in that area.
5	
6	## The owner asks in plain words — open the issue yourself, before the first commit
7	
8	Work here arrives as a chat request ("Maybe we can just put a 'Show list/Show Map'
9	toggle selector just under the filter…"), never as a filed issue. The
10	`task-lifecycle` check still wants a commit on the branch to reference one, so
11	**open the issue as your first step and put `Closes #N` in the original commit
12	message** — write it from the owner's own words, since it is the only record of
13	what was asked.
14	
15	Leaving it to the stop hook is the expensive path, and it is the path every
16	session took: 7 of the 12 sessions captured on 2026-07-29 declared the work done,
17	got blocked, and then paid create-issue + `git commit --amend` +
18	`git push --force-with-lease` + a second reply that added nothing (#134 33s,
19	#150 45s, #152 35s, #154 43s, #156 43s, #158 57s, #160 20s — ~4.6 min of pure
20	rework). Worse, by then the PR is already open, so the fix rewrites the commit
21	underneath it.
22	
23	## A dispatched run still has to classify its trigger comment
24	
25	The `comment-classification` check reads the last message addressed to you and
26	wants a `Comment class:` line in the reply to it. In a scheduled run that message
27	is the executor prompt ("Execute the Claudinite executor: …"), not anything the
28	owner wrote — but the check does not distinguish them, and it is BLOCKING at the
29	Stop hook. 19 of the sessions captured across 2026-07-29…07-31 were stopped by
30	exactly this finding, every one of them citing the dispatch prompt, and each paid
31	an extra closing reply to clear it (the two runs where the block lands at the end
32	and the cost is cleanly isolable: #183 115s, #160 121s).
33	
34	So **close a dispatched run's final reply with an explicit `Comment class:` line
35	classifying the dispatch itself** — `process-change` for an executor/scheduled-task
36	prompt — instead of discovering the requirement at Stop. On a real owner comment
37	the classification is the substance; on a dispatch it is a formality, but it is
38	far cheaper paid up front than as a second reply.
39	
40	## Read the PR's state, then merge — never loop on `enable_pr_auto_merge`
41	
42	`mcp__github__enable_pr_auto_merge` only accepts a PR whose required checks are
43	still **pending**. This repo's `ci.yml` runs on `pull_request` and finishes in
44	well under a minute, so by the time an agent reaches the arming step the PR is
45	usually already `clean` and the call errors — *"already in clean status (all
46	checks passed) … you can merge directly."* That is not a failure to work around:
47	take it as the answer and call `mcp__github__merge_pull_request` with `SQUASH`.
48	
49	The other refusal, *"in unstable status (required checks are failing)"*, is not a
50	verdict either — a check that is queued, or held at the Actions approval gate,
51	reads identically to one that failed. Re-read the PR
52	(`mcp__github__pull_request_read`) or the run list (`mcp__github__actions_list`)
53	to find out which, and never re-arm on a loop: PR #188 answered "unstable" and
54	then "clean" 27s later with nothing changed in between, and PR #182 answered
55	"unstable" three times across ~4 minutes before answering "clean".
56	
57	The cost is measured. The 2026-08-01 baselining run spent ~350s of its 765s — 4
58	arm attempts, 9 `pull_request_read`s and 5 `ScheduleWakeup` polls — circling PR
59	#182's merge state, and still ended without merging it; the owner merged it by
60	hand the next evening. The same morning's conversation-extract run took its one
61	refusal as an answer and squash-merged 22s later. Check state first, merge
62	directly when it is clean, and arm auto-merge only while checks are genuinely
63	pending.
64	
65	## Verifying UI changes visually (the `index.html` page and everything under `plan/`)
66	
67	Visual verification of the pages **is** available in this sandbox. Don't skip it
68	or downgrade to "verified by logic review only" claiming no browser exists — a
69	browser is here, and a UI change isn't done until it has been looked at.
70	
71	- Serve the repo and drive it with the preinstalled Chromium (or Playwright):
72	  `python3 -m http.server 8000`, then screenshot / click through
73	  `http://localhost:8000`. The app fetches `data/shows.json`, so it must be
74	  served over HTTP rather than opened as a file — and `localhost` bypasses the
75	  agent proxy, so the browser reaches the page even though external hosts need
76	  the proxy.
77	- **Launch Playwright with no `executablePath`, and import from `index.mjs`.**
78	  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers` is already exported in this
79	  sandbox, so `chromium.launch()` finds its browser on its own. Import the
80	  global build by its ESM entry —
81	  `import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'`
82	  (the sibling `index.js` is CJS, so a *named* import from it yields
83	  `undefined`) — or `$(npm root -g)/playwright/index.mjs` if the prefix moved.
84	  Path discovery and its sed-fix-up round-trips cost ~220s across five captured
85	  sessions, every one of them re-deriving the same two facts.
86	  `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium` is a **symlink** onto the version-pinned
87	  `chromium-<build>/chrome-linux/chrome`, so it is a valid `executablePath` if
88	  you ever need one — but you don't, and the build it points at moves with the
89	  image.
90	- **Never `npm i playwright` into the scratchpad to make the import resolve.**
91	  A bare `import { chromium } from 'playwright'` in a scratchpad script fails
92	  with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — the global install is not on the resolution
93	  path, and `NODE_PATH` does not apply to ESM, so exporting it changes nothing.
94	  The obvious next move is the wrong one: a fresh `npm i playwright` pulls a
95	  **newer** Playwright than the image's, which then hunts for a browser build
96	  the image does not ship (`chromium_headless_shell-1234` against the vendored
97	  `-1194`) and dies asking for `npx playwright install` — a download the
98	  sandbox cannot make. Three sessions on 2026-08-07 (#251, #258, #264) each
99	  took that detour and then backed out of it. Use the absolute path to the
100	  global build instead: it is the one matched to the vendored browsers.
101	- **Keep one browser driver script per session and re-point it.** Authoring a
102	  fresh throwaway Playwright script per screenshot cost 29 heredoc writes and
103	  ~7 minutes of wall clock across the captured sessions (one session alone: 16
104	  writes, 4.5 min). Write the driver once into the scratchpad, take the URL,
105	  selector and output path from `process.argv`, and re-run it — a re-run is
106	  seconds where a rewrite is 15–20s.
107	- To build a `/plan` favourites list for the render, a plain slug-per-line text
108	  file is accepted by the parser — pick shows spanning the statuses (and some
109	  same-day doubles) you want to eyeball.
110	- **Known-noisy console output from the served page.** A page driven off
111	  `python3 -m http.server` reliably logs a `favicon.ico` 404 (the repo ships
112	  none) and often `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` as the browser tears down. Neither
113	  is an application error — filter both out of a smoke script's error assertion
114	  so that a red run means something, rather than sending you chasing a phantom
115	  404 through extra browser runs.
116	- To match edfringe.com's live styling (e.g. the ticket-availability colours on
117	  the `/plan` grid), fetch the official site's CSS with `curl` through the agent
118	  proxy and read the palette out of it. `WebFetch` returns rendered text without
119	  the CSS, and headless Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy to reach an external
120	  host — `curl` is the one path that works for off-box assets.
121	
122	## The live site is reachable — check real state at `*.edfringenow.com`, allowing for CDN lag
123	
124	The environment's egress policy allows `*.edfringenow.com`, the live site's own
125	domain. So a question about what the deployed site actually serves — is the new
126	field in `data/shows.json`? did the deploy land? — is answerable directly, with
127	`curl https://www.edfringenow.com/…` through the agent proxy, rather than by
128	reasoning from the working tree. General egress is still closed: everything
129	*except* the allowed domain fails the same way, so this is a single-domain
130	window, not open internet.
131	
132	Two caveats before you trust what comes back:
133	
134	- **The response is CDN-cached, so a fresh push may not be visible yet.** A
135	  200 with stale content is not evidence the deploy failed — re-check after a
136	  delay, and never conclude "the change didn't ship" from one read taken
137	  seconds after the push.
138	- **Confirm the allowance is live in *your* session before relying on it.** The
139	  policy is per-environment and a session can be running under an older one; on
140	  2026-08-07 a probe of both `www.edfringenow.com` and the apex returned
141	  `curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403`. A 403 at CONNECT is a policy
142	  denial, not a site outage — `curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status"`
143	  lists the recent rejections and confirms which it is. When it's denied, say so
144	  and fall back to the repo, rather than reporting the live site as down.
145	
146	As with the off-box CSS fetch above, `curl` is the working path: headless
147	Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy, and `WebFetch` returns rendered text rather
148	than the raw JSON or asset you usually want here.
149	
150	## Watching a workflow or scheduler run — ask the MCP Actions tools, never poll with `curl`
151	
152	A run's state comes from `mcp__github__actions_get` / `mcp__github__actions_list`.
153	Do **not** poll `https://api.github.com/…` from the shell. `gh` is not installed
154	here, and shell egress to the API is a per-environment policy that has been
155	*denied* mid-session — and a denied `CONNECT` returns a proxy error body rather
156	than JSON, so an `until`-loop testing `.status == "completed"` neither
157	terminates nor says why. Both sessions that reached for it on 2026-08-07 lost
158	the poll silently: #249 burned two round-trips on a `curl` that "never actually
159	worked" before the MCP call answered in 5s, and #251 backgrounded an
160	`until curl …; sleep 15; done`, abandoned it, and fell back to a blind
161	`sleep 90` — for a run `actions_get` reported *already complete* five seconds
162	later. The orphaned sleep then fired two `task-notification`s that had to be
163	explained away to the owner.
164	
165	So: ask the MCP tool, and if the run is still going ask it again. Never a blind
166	fixed sleep, and never a shell poll.
167	
168	## The site is two front-ends — cross-page behaviour goes in `shared/`
169	
170	The Now page (`index.html` + `js/app.js`) and the planner (`plan/` + `plan/plan.js`)
171	are separate front-ends, and `plan/lib/` is the planner's own engine, not a common
172	library. But both are now ES modules, so **anything that must behave the same on
173	both pages belongs in `shared/`** and is imported by each — never copy-pasted.
174	Both pages spell the import the same way (`../shared/geo.js` resolves to
175	`/shared/geo.js` from either), so moving a value there is a small change.
176	
177	What is still genuinely twinned (untangled the same way when next touched): the
178	header `debug v<version>` pill, the Now/Plan nav, and the haversine in
179	`plan/lib/travel.js` that was ported from `js/app.js`.
180	
181	A shared module needs **no** `package.json` to mark it as ESM: the pinned Node 22
182	detects module syntax in a `.js` file by itself, with no warning and no flag, so
183	`node --check` and the test suite both handle it. `plan/package.json` predates
184	that detection and its stated reason (silencing a module-detection warning) no
185	longer applies; it is harmless, so it stays, but do not copy it as a pattern —
186	the `edfringe-no-stray-package-json` check flags any other one.
187	`.js` and `.mjs` are both served as `text/javascript` by `python3 -m http.server`,
188	so the extension is a style choice — use `.js`, matching `plan/lib/`.
189	
190	A new top-level source dir must be added to `scripts/verify.sh`'s `git ls-files`
191	list, or nothing in it is ever parse-checked — the `edfringe-verify-sh-covers-source-dirs`
192	check catches an omission. Note that `git ls-files` only sees *tracked* files, so
193	a new file silently sits outside the syntax sweep until it is committed — the
194	"checked N files" count is not evidence your new file was among them.
195	
196	## `.claudinite/shared/` is generated output — never hand-resolve its conflicts, always take the fresher version
197	
198	## A pack rule or check encodes a *work procedure*, never product behaviour
199	
200	Rules and checks in `.claudinite/local/packs/` are about **how work is done here**
201	— the gate that must stay wired, the tool that must be launched a certain way, the
202	files that must move together. **Product behaviour is not a rule.** What the site
203	does — which ticket statuses count as unavailable, what the Now page shows, how
204	far "walkable" reaches — is a **requirement**, and it belongs in the requirements
205	spec (`product/requirements.md`, the `executable-requirements` pack) and its
206	tests, never in a pack's `rules`.
207	
208	The trap is that product behaviour reads exactly like a good check candidate: it
209	is deterministic, statically detectable, and genuinely worth enforcing, so a
210	prose-to-checks sweep will happily convert it. The 2026-07-30 sweep did: it turned
211	the `ticketStatus`-not-`soldOut` rule into an `edfringe-ticket-status-unavailable`
212	check, with a clean scoped parse and a see-it-fail proof against mutated real repo
213	content — a well-built check of the wrong kind, which the owner rejected on sight
214	("Rules shouldn't be about product requirements, only work procedures"). The
215	sibling conversion in the same PR, `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` ("the
216	offline self-test must stay wired into `verify.sh`"), was the right kind and
217	stayed.
218	
219	Apply the test **before** writing the check, since the build quality of the check
220	tells you nothing about whether it belongs: *if the product changed its mind
221	tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* If yes it is a requirement — a red check
222	would then be reporting a product decision as a process violation, and the
223	requirements spec is where that decision is already supposed to live. If instead
224	it would still hold because it describes how we work regardless of what the
225	product does, it is a rule. Prose in a `RULES.md` gets the same test: the
226	`ticketStatus` paragraph in the `edfringe-data` pack is background a scraper
227	editor needs, not a rule, and it is not convertible.
228	
229	## Retiring a practice: delete it, state the rule that replaces it, don't narrate the change
230	
231	When a practice is withdrawn, the docs that taught it get **rewritten into the
232	current rule in the present tense** — not amended with a paragraph explaining what
233	used to be done and why it stopped. The owner's words on PR #240: *"make sure the
234	rules and comments are describing current state, not past changes. Describe the
235	rules, not the history."*
236	
237	The first pass at retiring the `probe-edfringe-api` skill did the opposite, and
238	every part of it read as diligence at the time: the pack `RULES.md`, its `README.md`
239	and `scraper/SCRAPING.md` each gained a passage narrating the retired probe practice
240	so a future reader would understand the ban. All of it came back out on review. A
241	reader who never knew the practice does not need to be taught it in order to be told
242	the rule, and describing it is how a withdrawn technique keeps getting rediscovered.
243	
244	The same pass also added a new `edfringe-workflows-allowlisted` check — every file
245	under `.github/workflows/` had to sit on a named allowlist — built properly, with
246	red-first fixtures and a live gate over the real tree. The owner removed it too:
247	retiring one practice is not the moment to install a guard against it. State the
248	rule; a check earns its place on its own, from a mistake that actually repeats, not
249	as the enforcement arm of the deletion that prompted it.
250	
251	This does **not** ban evidence. The measured costs cited throughout this file are
252	what argue a rule is worth its space, and they stay. What goes is narration of a
253	*superseded* way of working: the rule is what the reader needs, and the history
254	belongs to the commit that removed it.
255

1	# claude-code-web-users-support — for the people working on this from the web
2	
3	A Claude Code **web** session runs for a signed-in person, in a managed container. A
4	terminal session does neither. This pack is where the capabilities that depend on that
5	difference live — anything a project can offer only when the session knows **who** is
6	here.
7	
8	## Personal interaction preferences
9	
10	This project reads each person's **personal interaction preferences** at session start:
11	how they want to be worked with — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, the
12	phrases they use to trigger a defined command. If the current user has a file in the
13	store, its contents are already in this session's context, injected under this pack's
14	marker by [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs).
15	
16	**They are not project conventions.** Conventions belong to the packs that own each
17	subject and load as prose. What this carries is *personal*: the same rules travel with
18	a person across every project they work in, and two people on one project can want
19	different things. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project
20	convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the preference owns only the
21	trigger phrase.
22	
23	**The pack holds an address, not the content.** Preferences belong to a group of people
24	rather than to any one repository, so this project's declaration names the **store** —
25	a repo, and a path inside it holding one `<email>.md` per person:
26	
27	```json
28	{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
29	```
30	
31	`path` is optional and defaults to `preferences`. Reading is **local-first**: when this
32	repo *is* the store, the working copy wins over the default branch, so an edit in
33	progress is what the session sees.
34	
35	**Every miss is fail-soft.** No identity (a terminal session has none), no configured
36	store, no file for this person, a fetch that fails — each is one plain-text note and the
37	session proceeds on default interaction behavior. Nothing here is load-bearing, and a
38	nice-to-have must never be able to stop a session from starting.
39	
40	### Adding or changing a preference
41	
42	Edit that person's file **in the store repo** — never here, and never in the canon. One
43	distilled preference per bullet, in the imperative: a preference is a rule the assistant
44	can act on, not a description of a mood. A preference that turns out to be a project
45	convention in disguise belongs in the pack that owns its subject instead.

2	name: merge-to-main
3	description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
4	---
5	
6	
7	The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.
8	
9	**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.
10	
11	## Recipe (~4 calls)
12	
13	1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
14	2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
15	3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
16	4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
17	5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
18	
19	The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.
20	
21	## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)
22	
23	Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
24	`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.
25	
26	## Don't
27	
28	- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

2	name: git-github-advanced
3	description: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
4	---
5	
6	# Portable git & GitHub procedures
7	
8	The project-agnostic half of how we drive GitHub: the branch/commit-history rules for PR work, the CI-trigger rules, and how we keep merge-conflict churn cheap across parallel branches. (The issue → branch → PR task lifecycle that every task follows lives in [RULES.md](../../../../packs/basics/RULES.md), the `basics` baseline every project declares and every session loads — it's not task-gated, so it doesn't live here.) Project-specific GitHub procedures (the merge-to-main command, when to open a PR early, the merge-cheaply poll loop tuned to the local environment, and the generated-file merge rules) live in the consuming repo's own GitHub-procedures doc.
9	
10	## Updating an issue's status: comment, don't overwrite
11	
12	To post a **status update** on an issue (the lifecycle's "update the issue's status" step), use `add_issue_comment`. **Don't** reach for `issue_write` with `method: update` — that edits the issue itself and **replaces the whole body**, silently wiping the original description. Reserve `issue_write`/`update` for genuinely editing the issue (retitling, rewriting the body on purpose).
13	
14	## Branch and commit history
15	
16	### Commit often, in layers
17	
18	While working a branch, commit frequently rather than landing one big commit at the end — small, ordered commits let the owner follow the work as it develops. Use commits to *layer* the work in the order you'd want it reviewed:
19	
20	- Write the failing test(s) first, commit them, **then** implement the feature — so the history shows the contract before the code that satisfies it (and you've seen the test fail before trusting it, per [the basics pack's RULES.md](../../../basics/RULES.md)).
21	- Keep any documentation update as its own commit *after* the feature, not folded into it.
22	
23	There's no cost to a branch carrying many commits when the project uses a **squash** merge to `main` (one commit per PR): the squash collapses them into a single commit on `main`, so `main`'s one-commit-per-PR history is unaffected no matter how granularly the branch is committed.
24	
25	- **One caveat, at merge time: before rebasing an *unmerged* multi-commit branch onto a *moved* base, collapse commits that rewrite the same lines into one.** When your own commits churn the same lines (build X → refactor → remove X, common in an iterative design session) and the base has advanced, rebasing the stack replays *every* intermediate conflict against the new base. The squash-merge discards those commits anyway, so collapse them first — `git reset --soft $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)` then one fresh commit, and rebase that single commit: one conflict pass, not N. Lossless (unlike `reset --hard` + redo) and simpler than `--onto` when you want a single commit anyway.
26	
27	- Don't rewrite published/shared history to satisfy a tooling or authorship check (e.g. a hook flagging "unverified" commits): only amend your own un-pushed branch commits. Commits already on a shared branch — including ones merged in from `main` — belong to that history; reset-authoring or rebasing them forks your branch away from it.
28	- After your commit is **squash-merged** to `main`, a *reused* feature branch still carries that original commit (the squash created a *new* commit on `main`, so the branch's own is unreachable from it) — and the next PR off the branch re-includes it in the diff, because the three-dot merge-base predates the squash. Sync the branch to `origin/main` before opening the next PR (`git rebase origin/main`, which drops the commit as an already-applied cherry-pick, or a hard reset): it's your own un-merged branch, so this is the amend-your-own-commits case above, not rewriting shared history.
29	  - **`git rebase origin/main` only drops the old commit cleanly when the branch carried a *single* squash-merged commit.** When it carried *several* commits that `main` squashed into *one* (then kept developing), git can't match them to the squash as already-applied, so it replays them and conflicts mid-rebase. Replant only the genuinely-new commits instead: `git rebase --onto origin/main <last-squash-merged-commit>` (then `git push --force-with-lease`). If the new work is small, a `git reset --hard origin/main` + redo beats fighting the replay.
30	  - **If the merge auto-deleted the remote branch, start follow-up work on a new branch off `origin/main`** rather than reusing the old name — it has no stale tracking ref and no rebase dance. If you do reuse the old name: `--force-with-lease` actively *fails* — `git push --force-with-lease` rejects with `stale info` then `couldn't find remote ref <branch>` because the lease expects a remote branch that no longer exists. There's nothing to overwrite, so `git fetch --prune` (drop the stale tracking ref) then a plain `git push -u origin <branch>` just recreates it.
31	
32	## An automated commit-nag is not authorization to commit drift
33	
34	An automated prompt to commit the working tree (a stop-hook, a CI nag) tells you the tree is dirty — not that the changes are yours or intended. Before obeying, inspect what actually changed (`git status` / `git diff`): if it's environment/setup drift — a submodule pointer moved by `git submodule update` at clone time, a lockfile a setup script regenerated, generated artifacts — revert it rather than committing it onto your branch. Committing drift slips an unintended dependency or generated-file bump into an unrelated change.
35	
36	## Open a PR early when the reviewable artifact only exists on CI
37	
38	The default is to hold a PR until asked. Reverse that when a change's only reviewable output is produced by CI — an e2e/heavy-browser run, or a rendered artifact (a UI-snapshot pixel diff, a generated gallery) that can't be exercised in the local sandbox. Opening the PR is how the change is seen working and how failures surface, so doing it up front — rather than iterating locally first, which proves nothing for these classes — is the faster path to a working, reviewable result. Each CI iteration costs a full round-trip, so get the first one running as early as possible.
39	
40	## Never `git checkout <ref> -- <paths>` to carry uncommitted edits onto another branch
41	
42	It reads those paths out of `<ref>`'s **committed** tree and writes them over the working copy — so the uncommitted edits you were trying to move are destroyed, silently and unrecoverably (no reflog, no stash). Move in-progress work either by branching in place (`git checkout -b <new>`, which carries a dirty tree with it) or by committing/stashing first and then restoring on the new branch. In particular never put the checkout in the same `&&` chain as the branch creation: by the time it runs, the edits are already the only copy.
43	
44	## Sync early to keep merge conflicts small
45	
46	Conflict size scales with how long a branch lives and how far it drifts from the default branch. Sync early rather than at the end: when starting work on a branch — and periodically while it's open — bring the latest default branch in first, so the branch carries current sources instead of discovering the gap at merge time. A one-commit-per-PR squash history already keeps each branch a single reviewable unit, so shorter-lived, freshly-synced branches are the norm.
47	
48	**In a repo that forbids merge commits on the branch — the `squash-merge-history` check, or squash-only merging generally — sync by *rebasing*, never `git merge` the base in.** A `git merge origin/main` (even just to resolve conflicts) leaves a **merge commit** the check blocks, forcing a redo; `git pull --rebase` / `git rebase origin/main` replays your work with no merge commit. GitHub's **"Update branch"** button — and the `update_pull_request_branch` API behind it — is this same base-merge in disguise: it adds exactly the merge commit the check blocks, so refresh with a local rebase + `git push --force-with-lease` instead. The merge-conflict-resolution gotchas below apply to a rebase's conflicts exactly the same way.
49	
50	## After a remote-side merge, fetch before branching off origin/main
51	
52	A GitHub API/UI (or any remote-side) merge does **not** advance your local `origin/main` — it stays at the pre-merge commit until you `git fetch`. Branching off `origin/main` immediately after a remote merge forks the pre-merge state, silently missing the just-merged work; symptoms surface later as a missing file or a failed `git mv` on the new branch. Fix: `git fetch origin main` before creating the branch.
53	
54	## `git pull` failing "refusing to merge unrelated histories" usually means upstream re-rooted
55	
56	When syncing a long-lived local clone's default branch fails with `refusing to merge unrelated histories` (often alongside `ahead N, behind M`), the usual cause is that upstream **re-rooted** the branch — a history rewrite replaced the root commit — not repository corruption. Do **not** reach for `--allow-unrelated-histories`: that "fix" welds the two histories together into a merge nobody wants. Instead inspect what the local side uniquely holds (`git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` — typically just the old root), keep anything real by rebasing it onto the new history, then `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`. A work branch created from *fetched* refs is unaffected; only stale local refs from before the rewrite hit this.
57	
58	## A conformance finding on history you didn't write may be a stale diff base — refresh before fixing
59	
60	A Stop-hook or CI conformance check diffs your branch against `origin/main`. In a fresh cloud sandbox that ref can be **stale** — behind real `main` by whole merged PRs — so the check reads the wrong base and can flag findings on commits or code you never touched. Before acting on a finding you don't recognize, `git fetch origin <default-branch>` and re-run: a stale-base phantom disappears, and whatever survives against the current base is real — fix that. (The same stale ref bases new work on outdated product code, so fetch before building against `main`, too.)
61	
62	The same reflex applies when a **real** (not phantom) red check blocks *your* PR and you've correctly pinned it as pre-existing and unrelated to your diff: that "not mine" diagnosis is a **sync-the-base** signal, not a fix-it-yourself-or-ask-the-user one — `main` has often *already fixed* it since you branched, so merge/rebase the latest base into your branch and re-check before proposing a fix or escalating.
63	
64	## In a squash-merge repo, "commits ahead of main" does not mean "unmerged"
65	
66	A squash-merge creates a new commit on `main` that the branch's own commits are unreachable from, so a branch whose work has already landed still shows ahead by N. **"Ahead by N" never alone means unmerged.** Determine real status by content, not raw count:
67	
68	1. **PR state** — a merged PR means the work is in `main`; safe to delete however many commits show ahead.
69	2. **Content diff** — `git diff --stat main..branch`: if everything the branch adds is already in `main`, the work landed (catches a squash with no surviving PR).
70	3. **Superseded elsewhere** — the branch's work may have landed in `main` under a *different path or form* (a doc distilled into another, a feature re-implemented), so a file/line diff still shows its additions as branch-side and it reads as unmerged. Before concluding so, check whether its *intent* already exists in `main` — grep for the concept, not just the exact path.
71	4. **No merge-base** — `git merge-base` fails when a force-push rewrote `main` and orphaned the branch; can't be proven in or out mechanically; needs human review, never an automatic delete.
72	5. Otherwise — genuine unmerged work.
73	
74	## A push or PR made with the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not start another workflow
75	
76	GitHub suppresses workflow runs triggered by the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to prevent recursion, so a workflow's own `git push` or `gh pr create` won't fire another workflow (e.g. a `test` or cache-refresh workflow). The one exception is `workflow_dispatch` / `repository_dispatch` — which is why an automation pipeline that needs the downstream checks to run must dispatch them explicitly. A run dispatched against a branch executes on its head commit, so its checks still attach to the PR. The same suppression covers a Claude session's own app-scoped pushes: creating a PR through the API does fire its `pull_request` run, but a follow-up push to that PR gets **no** `synchronize` run — so don't wait for checks that will never start on the new head; gate by running the CI commands locally, and rely on the post-merge run (merging through the merge API does fire the `push` workflow on the default branch).
77	
78	**"Suppressed" is not always "absent", and the difference decides whether a PR can merge.** Where the repo requires approval for a workflow run, GitHub *creates* the `pull_request` run and parks it at conclusion `action_required` with **zero jobs**, waiting for a human "Approve and run" that unattended automation never gets. The run never executes and never reports, yet it still counts against the PR: `mergeable_state` stays `unstable` and auto-merge refuses to arm, even though the explicitly dispatched run on the same head sha passed. Nothing inside the workflow file can prevent it — `branches`/`branches-ignore` on `pull_request` filter the **base** branch (a bot branch's PR still targets the default branch), and the approval gate is applied to the whole run before any job-level `if` is evaluated. So treat a gated run as **no verdict rather than a failure**, and land the PR on the evidence of the run that actually ran.
79	
80	## A workflow definition only takes effect once it's on the default branch
81	
82	A `workflow_dispatch` or scheduled workflow runs from the copy on the **default branch**, and a `pull_request` run uses the workflow files from the PR's **base** branch — so a workflow you only added on a feature branch isn't dispatchable, and a build/CI change doesn't apply, until it's merged. Merge workflow and build-script changes *before* the release or run that depends on them, or that run executes the *old* definition (shipping a stale build, or silently skipping a check you thought you'd added). This is distinct from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` recursion rule above: even a human-triggered run reads the definition from the default/base branch, not your feature branch.
83	
84	## A CI OIDC `sub` claim is matched case-sensitively by the cloud trust policy
85	
86	GitHub's OIDC `sub` uses the repository's **canonical casing** (`repo:Owner/Repo:ref:…`), and a cloud trust policy compares it exactly — AWS IAM `StringEquals` is case-sensitive — so a trust policy written with the wrong case fails with a bare `Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` and **no** hint that casing is the cause. Match the exact canonical `owner/repo` (or list both casings in the condition). The same exact-match caution applies to any OIDC-federated cloud, not just AWS.
87	
88	## An automated job needs a unique branch per run
89	
90	An automated or scheduled job that derives its branch name from a non-unique key (e.g. the date) collides with itself on a repeat run for that key — `git checkout -b` fails when the branch already exists, and a push to the diverged remote branch is rejected non-fast-forward (so the run can't even open its PR). Give every run its own branch: append a per-run-unique suffix (`$RANDOM` / a short token) to the readable prefix.
91	
92	## An unattended workflow must escalate its own failure to a human-visible state
93	
94	A workflow with no human watching the run — scheduled, triggered by a push/merge, or a fire-and-forget manual dispatch, with no other path that reaches a person — must converge a failure to something a human will see (e.g. open a `workflow-failure` issue for it) rather than merely exiting red in the Actions list, where nobody looks. Skip this only when the failure is already loud: a `pull_request`/push CI run that blocks merge with a red required check the author is watching, or a workflow that already flags the triggering issue itself on failure. The canon's [report-failure](../../../../.github/actions/report-failure/action.yml) action does exactly this — a **fresh** issue per failure, with earlier open failure issues for the same workflow closed as duplicates of the newest — so the current failure is always the single open bug to triage; a standing per-workflow issue appended to on each failure is an equally valid shape, the invariant is only that the red run reaches a person.
95	
96	When the escalation is itself a separate reusable workflow invoked via `workflow_call`, permissions don't propagate implicitly through the chain: the job that calls it needs the permission explicitly granted (e.g. `issues: write`), and if that reusable workflow in turn calls another one, the middle workflow must forward the same grant to its own call — a caller two levels up granting it once is not enough.
97	
98	## A CI job that inspects commit shape must check out the PR head, not the merge ref
99	
100	On `pull_request`, `actions/checkout` checks out the synthetic `refs/pull/N/merge` commit by default — an ephemeral merge of the PR head into the base — so `HEAD` is itself a merge commit, not the branch tip. Any job that reasons about commit *shape* or history (merge commits, commit count, `--first-parent`, commit messages) reads that synthetic merge and misfires: a "no merge commits" check false-positives even on a linear branch, since `HEAD` is a merge. Check out the head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}`) so CI evaluates the same branch tip a local run does.
101	
102	## To read a PR's CI result, look at its check runs — `get_status` misses Actions
103	
104	GitHub **Actions** reports results as **check runs**, not the legacy **commit statuses**, so `pull_request_read` `method: get_status` returns `state: pending`, `total_count: 0` for a PR whose Actions CI has already **passed** — reading falsely as "no CI / not started," which can skip a real gate or trigger an endless wait. Gate on CI by reading the **check runs for the PR head SHA** (`get_check_run`, or the workflow run for that SHA) instead. Target the head SHA directly rather than `actions_list`-ing the repo's runs — that returns every run, its output is huge, and a specific check-run/SHA query is both correct and cheap.
105	
106	## To confirm a non-PR run (push / dispatch), read its job logs — it has no PR check runs
107	
108	A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.
109	
110	## Mark large committed fixtures `linguist-vendored` to fix language stats
111	
112	Large committed fixture files (full-page HTML, generated data dumps) can dwarf actual source by byte count and cause GitHub to mislabel the repo's primary language. Add a `.gitattributes` entry for each such path (e.g. `test/fixtures/*.html linguist-vendored`) to tell Linguist to ignore it; apply the same annotation whenever you add another large generated or fixture file.
113	
114	## Renaming a directory that houses a submodule
115	
116	`git mv` on a directory containing a submodule rewrites `.gitmodules` and the index correctly but leaves `.git/config` stale — its old `[submodule "<old/path>"]` entry lingers, so any operation that consults `.git/config` (submodule status, checkout) sees the old path until you fix it. Run `git submodule sync && git submodule update --init` after the move to propagate the new path and re-register the submodule.
117	
118	## GitHub Markdown inside a `<td>` requires surrounding blank lines
119	
120	In a GitHub-rendered Markdown file, cmark-gfm re-enters Markdown mode inside a raw `<td>` only when blank lines surround the cell's content — without them the cell is treated as a raw HTML block and its content is shown verbatim (no `![img]()`, no `**bold**`, no links). GitHub's sanitizer strips `style` / CSS, so a flexbox two-column layout won't render; use a plain `<table>` with `align` / `valign` / `width` instead. GFM pipe-table cells can't hold multi-line prose — use the raw-`<table>` form when a cell needs it. A leading inline `<!-- … -->` comment also opens an HTML block, so keep any such marker as the *last* token on the line, leaving the line to *start* as Markdown.
121	
122	## `commit.gpgsign = true` does not cover merge commits
123	
124	`commit.gpgsign = true` signs ordinary commits but does not apply to `git merge` — each merge produces an unsigned commit even with signing fully configured. In a repo that enforces commit verification, this requires a fix-up after the fact. Cover merges proactively: either pass `-S` to every `git merge` call, or set `merge.gpgsign = true` globally so merges are signed the same way commits are.
125	
126	## When access is scoped to an explicit repo list, query per-repo — never an org/user-wide search
127	
128	A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.
129	
130	## Cap *and* qualify every list/search call — an unbounded one blows the tool-result limit
131	
132	A list or search API call that isn't bounded returns a full page of full-bodied records and overruns the agent's tool-result cap, which costs two or three further calls to dig the answer back out of the spilled result — a pure-overhead round trip on a call whose wanted answer was a single record. Two independent bounds, both needed:
133

139	## Merging gotchas
140	
141	These conflict/merge traps are independent of any one project's file layout.
142	
143	### Merging across a file relocation
144	
145	git's rename detection re-applies your content edits onto the moved files, but it does *not* fix *references* to the moved paths — an npm script, a `.gitattributes` glob, or a doc link naming the old location keeps pointing there and breaks with no conflict (a green local test on the old layout won't catch it either). After such a merge, grep the files your branch touched for the old paths.
146	
147	### Merging in content that predates a branch-wide invariant
148	
149	When your branch establishes a cross-cutting invariant — a renamed term, a "mentioned only in X" containment rule — a branch you merge in that *predates* it can silently reintroduce violations: its independent additions (a new file, a new section) auto-merge clean, no conflict, while still using the old form. Resolving the marked conflicts isn't enough. Re-run the check that *defines* the invariant (the grep) over the whole tree after the merge, not just the conflicted files.
150	
151	### Porting old work forward across a changed invariant
152	
153	The converse direction: when you re-implement or cherry-pick an *older* change onto current `main`, check each part against the invariants `main` has added since — not just whether it still applies. A part that violates a now-enforced guarantee becomes a **silent no-op** if taken verbatim (e.g. a guard that reverts any write outside an allowed set leaves the patch landed but doing nothing), so drop or redesign it rather than copy it.
